title: A systematic assessment of AI-assisted diagnostic interpretation in clinical practice
official: SAMURAI-Reader: systematic assessment of the medical utility of radiology and diagnostic artificial intelligence: multicase multireader studies
summary:
Background and study aims
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare to help doctors interpret tests like X-rays and ECGs. While these tools show promise, it is vital to check if they actually help doctors make better decisions in real-world practice. This study aims to evaluate whether using AI tools improves the accuracy, confidence, and speed of healthcare professionals when diagnosing conditions from medical data.

Who can participate?
Healthcare professionals (doctors, nurses and trainees) who routinely interpret diagnostic data as part of their job.

What does the study involve? 
Participants will log into a secure online platform to review cases. They will interpret a set of anonymous patient cases twice: once without AI help and, after a break, once with AI help. They will provide a diagnosis and rate their confidence. They will also complete surveys about their experience and attitudes toward AI.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The possible benefits of taking part include helping to evaluate AI-powered tools that may improve the accuracy, speed, and consistency of interpreting scans and other diagnostic data, which could in the future lead to better patient care and more efficient use of NHS resources. Participants may also find that the study provides useful feedback on their own practice and experience of using AI-assisted systems. The main risks and burdens relate to the time required to review anonymised cases, complete online surveys, and use the study platform alongside routine work; there are no direct clinical risks, as all data are de-identified and no treatment decisions for real patients will be based on study interpretations. Participation is entirely voluntary, and clinicians can withdraw at any time without giving a reason and without any impact on their employment or clinical role.

Where is the study run from?
Oxford Clinical Artificial Intelligence Research (OxCAIR), Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2026 to January 2029

Who is funding the study?
Oxford Clinical Artificial Intelligence Research (OxCAIR) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Abdala Trinidad Espinosa Morgado, abdala.espinosa@ouh.nhs.uk
conditions: Various medical conditions requiring diagnostic interpretation (e.g., radiology scans, ECGs, or other diagnostic data). The platform is designed to be modality-agnostic.

interventions.name:
1. Intervention: Interpretation of diagnostic data using an AI-powered clinical decision support tool. Participants (readers) are provided with automated analysis and suggested findings/diagnoses from the AI tool.
2. Comparator: Unaided interpretation (standard clinical practice) where participants

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Healthcare professionals (e.g., doctors, radiologists, specialist nurses, trainees) who routinely interpret the relevant diagnostic data as part of their clinical practice
2. Willing and able to provide informed consent
3. Sufficient proficiency in the language of the study platform
4. Access to required technology/internet to use the digital platform
5. Completion of required training/familiarization with the platform and AI tool
Exclusion criteria:
1. Inability or unwillingness to provide informed consent
2. Insufficient language proficiency
3. Lack of access to required technology

Additional exclusions may be defined per sub-study
